summary: This experimental document is a snapshot of Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol deployment scenarios. It discusses placement of the network elements LISP introduces, reflecting the working group's thinking as of Summer 2013.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7215 is a deployment guide for LISP, the idea of splitting a host's address into a fixed identifier and a changeable locator. It compares where the new routers can go, at the customer's own edge or at the provider's, and what each choice gains and costs, and it covers the transition arrangements that let ordinary sites reach LISP sites.

subtitle: Where to put the new LISP equipment in a real network, and what each placement costs you.

tldr.problem: LISP splits an address into a stable identifier and a locator, which means new equipment has to appear at the edge of every network that takes part, and each place to put it has drawbacks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through the placement options for tunnel routers, map servers and map resolvers, and the proxy tunnel routers used to reach LISP sites from the rest of the Internet during the transition.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that the authors describe as a snapshot of the working group's thinking as of Summer 2013. They say LISP is not recommended for deployment beyond experimental situations, and that there was no standardized security to implement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LISP is designed to address the scaling issues of the global Internet routing system identified in RFC 4984 by separating the current addressing scheme into Endpoint IDentifiers and Routing LOCators. The main protocol specification describes how the separation is achieved and which new network elements are introduced, and details the packet formats for the data and control planes.

LISP assumes that the separation is between the edge and the core and uses mapping and encapsulation for forwarding. While the boundary between the two is not strictly defined, one widely accepted definition places it at the border routers of stub autonomous systems, which may carry a partial or complete default-free zone routing table. The initial design took this location as a baseline. The applications go beyond decreasing the size of the default-free zone table and include improved multihoming and ingress traffic engineering support for edge networks, and even individual hosts. The memo uses the term LISP site for these networks or hosts behind a LISP tunnel router, and formally defines a network element as a facility or equipment used in the provision of a communications service over the Internet, and a LISP site as a single host or a set of network elements in an edge network under the administrative control of a single organization, delimited from other networks by LISP tunnel routers.

The memo is candid about its own standing. It describes itself as a snapshot of different LISP deployment scenarios representing the thinking of the LISP working group as of Summer 2013, and says that deployment scenarios may have evolved since then, so the document is one stable point in that evolution. It says LISP is not recommended for deployment beyond experimental situations, that results of experimentation may lead to modifications and enhancements of LISP mechanisms, and that at the time of writing there is no standardized security to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP separates the name of a host from the address that reaches it, and that means new routers have to sit at the edge of participating networks. The memo is a practical guide to where to put them. It is explicitly a snapshot of one working group's thinking from 2013, and it warns that the security story was not finished.

sections.title: Tunnel Routers and Where to Put Them
sections.content:
The device that is the gateway between the edge and the core is called a tunnel router. It performs one or both of two separate functions: encapsulating packets originating from an end host so they can be transported over intermediary networks towards the other endpoint, and decapsulating packets entering from intermediary networks that were originated at a remote host. The first function is performed by an Ingress Tunnel Router and the second by an Egress Tunnel Router.

The customer edge scenario places tunnel router functionality on the routers that connect the LISP site to its upstreams but are under its own control. The memo treats this as the reference location. Its main advantage from the site's point of view is direct control over ingress traffic engineering, which makes it easy to set up and maintain active/active, active/backup or more complex policies, adding ISPs and additional tunnel routers at will, without involving third parties. Because everything is under the same administrative control, reachability information of all egress routers is easier to synchronize, since the necessary control traffic can be allowed between their locators, so the Locator-Status-Bits can be set correctly. Placing the tunnel router at the edge of the site also means existing internal network configuration does not need to be modified: firewall rules, router configurations and address assignments inside the site stay unchanged, which helps with incremental deployment. The drawback is MTU: encapsulation adds overhead and lowers the effective end-to-end path MTU, and some transit networks provide larger MTU values than the typical 1500 bytes of common access technologies.

The provider edge scenario places the routers in the service provider's network. The main incentive is that the customer does not have to upgrade its own routers or change the configuration of any equipment, and for a large provider this can mean upgrading a few routers rather than many. The site loses one of the main benefits of LISP, ingress traffic engineering, because the provider controls the egress routers and customers would need extra complexity to modify their mapping entries. The problem is worse when the site is multihomed, because the customer must ask both providers for changes and they are unlikely to apply them at the same time, which can leave the site's mappings inconsistent. Since the routers sit in different administrative domains, locator reachability information is unlikely to be exchanged among them, making the Locator-Status-Bits hard to set correctly, so their use is discouraged. Compared with the customer edge, the provider edge may diminish MTU issues because the tunnel router is closer to the core, where links typically have higher MTUs.

The memo also covers tunnel routers behind network address translation. Packets encapsulated by an ingress tunnel router are just UDP packets from the point of view of a NAT device. Map-Requests, however, have a different 5-tuple in the IP header than the Map-Reply generated by the authoritative egress router, so no state is matched in the NAT table and the packet is dropped; the NAT device must send all UDP packets with source port 4342 to the ingress router's locator and rewrite the address family identifier and originating router locator fields in the payload. An egress tunnel router behind NAT is reachable by the Internet-facing locator of the NAT device, so it needs to know that locator and configure a loopback interface with it, which means LISP equipment needs support for dynamic locators in the mapping database. Both cases support only one tunnel router behind the NAT device, and the memo concludes that LISP sites cannot be behind carrier-based NATs, since two different sites would collide on the same forwarded UDP port, and that deployments behind NAT should be avoided if possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel router is the box that wraps outgoing packets and unwraps incoming ones. Put it in your own network and you keep control of how traffic enters and leaves, and nothing inside has to change. Put it in the provider's network and you avoid touching your own equipment, but you give up that control and the provider has to coordinate changes across competing operators.

sections.title: Map-Servers and Map-Resolvers
sections.content:
Map-Servers and Map-Resolvers make up the LISP mapping system and provide a means of finding authoritative EID-to-RLOC mapping information. They are meant to be deployed in locator space, and their operation behind NAT is not supported.

A Map-Server learns EID-to-RLOC mapping entries from an authoritative source and publishes them in the distributed mapping database. These entries are learned through authenticated Map-Register messages sent by authoritative egress routers. On reception of a Map-Request, the Map-Server verifies that the destination EID matches an EID-Prefix for which it is authoritative and then re-encapsulates and forwards it to a matching egress router. The Map-Server is provided by a Mapping Service Provider, which participates in the global distributed mapping database infrastructure by setting up connections to other participants according to the mapping system employed, such as the Alternative Logical Topology or the Delegated Database Tree. Participation and the storing of mapping data are subject to the policies of the root operators, who should check ownership rights for the EID-Prefixes stored by participants.

The Delegated Database Tree is used by providers to give reachability between their Map-Resolvers and Map-Servers. Its root is operated by a collection of organizations on an open basis, and, as with the DNS root, it has several server instances named after Greek letters and operated by independent organizations. When this document was published there were six such instances, one of them anycasted. The root and the mapping providers rely on the allocation policies defined by Regional Internet Registries to determine prefix ownership for use as EIDs. A Map-Server plays a key role in the reachability of the prefixes it serves: it publishes them into the distributed mapping database, and it encapsulates and forwards Map-Requests to the authoritative egress routers. Ingress routers encapsulating towards EIDs for which a failed Map-Server is responsible will be unable to look up any of their covering prefixes, the only exceptions being those that already hold the mappings in their local caches, which lets them reach egress routers until the entry expires, typically after 24 hours. Redundant Map-Server deployments are therefore desirable, and a set of Map-Servers providing high-availability service to the same set of prefixes is called a redundancy group. Egress routers are configured to send Map-Register messages to all Map-Servers in the group.

A Map-Resolver accepts LISP-encapsulated Map-Requests, typically from an ingress router, and finds the appropriate mapping by consulting the distributed mapping database. Anyone with access to the database can set one up. For performance reasons it is recommended that LISP sites use Map-Resolvers topologically close to their ingress routers. In medium to large networks the ingress routers must be configured with the resolver's locator, which can be done manually, but in small office and home office scenarios a mechanism for autoconfiguration should be provided. One solution for sites of any size is the use of anycast locators for Map-Resolvers, similar to the DNS root server infrastructure; since LISP uses UDP encapsulation, anycast would not affect reliability. LISP routers can then be shipped with a preconfigured list of well-known resolver locators that an administrator can edit.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping system has two halves. The map server holds the authoritative list of which locators serve which identifiers, and publishes it into a shared database. The map resolver looks up an answer in that database on behalf of an ingress router. A resolver placed near the ingress routers answers faster, so anycast addresses let several resolvers share one name.

sections.title: Proxy Tunnel Routers
sections.content:
Proxy Ingress Tunnel Routers are part of the non-LISP to LISP transition mechanism, allowing non-LISP sites to reach LISP sites. They announce via BGP certain EID-Prefixes, aggregated whenever possible, to attract traffic from non-LISP sites towards EIDs in the covered range. They do the mapping system lookup and encapsulate received packets towards the appropriate egress router. In the reverse path, LISP sites can reach non-LISP sites by simply not encapsulating traffic. A LISP site needs an interworking mechanism to be reachable from non-LISP sites, and a Proxy Ingress Tunnel Router can fulfil this role, enabling early adopters to see the benefits of LISP in a similar way to tunnel brokers helping the transition from IPv4 to IPv6. To be reachable from non-LISP sites the site has two options: keep announcing its prefixes with BGP, or have a proxy ingress tunnel router announce prefixes covering them. If the goal of reducing the default-free zone table size is to be reached, the second option is preferred, and it also allows LISP-based ingress traffic engineering from all sites.

Proxy Egress Tunnel Routers, in contrast, are not required for the correct functioning of all LISP sites. There are two cases where they help. The first is LISP sites with unicast reverse path forwarding restrictions: when forwarding traffic to non-LISP sites an ingress router does not encapsulate packets, leaving the original IP headers intact, so packets have EIDs in their source address, and the provider's edge router may fail the reverse path filtering check because the next hop is not on the interface towards the customer router. To avoid this, the affected ingress router encapsulates packets towards the locator of the proxy egress router for non-LISP destinations, so the source address seen by the edge router is the ingress router's locator, and the proxy egress router then decapsulates and forwards the packets.

The second use case is IPv4 to IPv6 transition. Service providers using older access network hardware that only supports IPv4 can still offer IPv6 to their clients by providing a customer premises device running LISP and proxy egress routers for accessing IPv6-only non-LISP sites and LISP sites with IPv6-only locators. Packets from the client LISP site for those destinations are encapsulated towards the proxy egress router's IPv4 locator, which is in a native IPv6 network where it decapsulates and forwards them.

Proxy egress routers may introduce path stretch, the ratio between the cost of the selected path and that of the optimal path, so the provider has to weigh using several devices close to the customers against fewer devices farther away. Since the deployment incentives for the two kinds of proxy router differ, they are likely to be deployed in separate devices, except in the content delivery network case, which may deploy both in a single device. Their existence involves another step in configuring a LISP router, and customer premises routers, which are typically configured by DHCP, stand to benefit most. Autoconfiguration of the proxy egress router locator could be achieved by a DHCP option or by adding a field to either Map-Notify or Map-Reply messages.
sections.plainLanguage: While the transition is under way, ordinary sites have to be able to reach LISP sites. A proxy ingress router does that: it advertises the LISP prefix in the ordinary routing system, looks up the real destination, and forwards the packet the LISP way. A proxy egress router is the mirror image, for the cases where a LISP site needs to reach ordinary sites without upsetting the provider's checks.

sections.title: Migration to LISP
sections.content:
The memo discusses a deployment architecture to support the migration to a LISP-enabled Internet, using the loosely defined terms early transition phase, late transition phase and LISP Internet phase for the periods when LISP sites are a minority, a majority, or represent all edge networks.

For sites wishing to migrate with their provider-independent prefix, the least disruptive way is to upgrade their border routers to support LISP and register the prefix into the mapping system, but to keep announcing it with BGP as well. LISP sites then reach them over LISP while legacy sites are unaffected. The main disadvantage is that no decrease in the default-free zone table size is achieved, though increasing the number of LISP sites is still an important gain, since a higher ratio of LISP to non-LISP sites may decrease the need for BGP-based traffic engineering that leads to prefix deaggregation, which in turn may decrease the table size and churn in the late transition phase.

Providers with enough transit capacity can offer proxy ingress tunnel router service to their clients as a separate service. The provider announces the prefix into the default-free zone and the client gets ingress traffic engineering without prefix deaggregation, at the price of added path stretch. Routing all non-LISP ingress traffic through a third party that is not one of its own providers is only feasible for sites with modest amounts of traffic, especially in the first stage of the transition, because the handling of that traffic is likely to result in additional costs passed down to the client.

Proxy-ITR Route Distribution outsources the BGP announcement of EIDs to a third party, a proxy ingress tunnel router service provider, which manages a set of distributed proxy routers that advertise the corresponding EID-Prefixes through BGP and then encapsulate the traffic they receive towards the locators of the LISP site. The architecture requires no modification to existing LISP network elements but introduces a new conceptual element, the EID-Route Server, a router that either propagates routes learned from other EID-Route Servers or originates EID-Routes, and it is worth noting that a BGP-capable router can also be considered an EID-Route Server. The EID-Routes it originates are those for which it is authoritative, and it propagates them to proxy ingress routers within its own autonomous system. The architecture decouples EID origination from route propagation, which lets it represent business relationships between proxy router operators accurately, makes it more mapping system agnostic, and makes only minor changes to the proxy ingress tunnel router implementation. Its flexibility and scalability do not come without a cost, since a proxy router service provider has to establish either transit or peering relationships to improve its connectivity.

The memo closes with a table of the expected effect of each scenario on the default-free zone table size. In the early transition phase, LISP with BGP produces no change while the other two produce a slower increase. In the late transition phase, LISP with BGP may decrease the table while the other two still produce a slower increase. In the LISP Internet phase, both the provider proxy service and route distribution produce a considerable decrease. It expects proxy route distribution to coexist with LISP with BGP during the migration, with the latter more popular early on.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to get a LISP prefix into the ordinary routing system while the transition happens: keep announcing it yourself with BGP, have your provider announce it for you, or hire a third party whose routers announce it on your behalf. The table at the end of the memo says which of them helps the global routing table most as more sites move over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo is brief. All security implications of LISP deployments are to be discussed in separate documents: the LISP threats document gives an overview of LISP threat models, including egress router operators attracting traffic by overclaiming an EID-Prefix, and securing mapping lookups is discussed in the LISP security document.

The introduction adds that at the time of writing there was no standardized security to implement, and warns that there were no countermeasures for any of the threats identified in the threats document. It points to the section of the main LISP specification listing known issues that need further work during development, implementation and experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo leaves security to other documents and says plainly that at the time it was written there was nothing standard to implement and no countermeasures for the known threats.

items.title: Tunnel Router (xTR)
items.text: The gateway between the edge and the core. It encapsulates outgoing packets, decapsulates incoming ones, or both.

items.title: Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR)
items.text: Encapsulates packets from an end host so they can travel across intermediary networks.

items.title: Egress Tunnel Router (ETR)
items.text: Decapsulates packets arriving from intermediary networks that were originated at a remote host.

items.title: Map-Server
items.text: Learns EID-to-RLOC mappings from authoritative sources and publishes them in the distributed mapping database.

items.title: Map-Resolver
items.text: Answers mapping lookups by consulting the distributed mapping database on behalf of an ingress router.

items.title: Proxy Ingress Tunnel Router
items.text: Makes a LISP site reachable from non-LISP sites by announcing its prefixes and encapsulating the traffic.

items.title: Proxy Egress Tunnel Router
items.text: Lets a LISP site reach non-LISP sites where reverse path filtering or address family differences get in the way.
